newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian backbencher calls for native title plan.
newsitem.headline: Australian backbencher calls for native title plan.

text.p: A senior backbench member of the Australian government criticised Prime Minister John Howard for refusing to release his detailed plan to resolve the current dispute over native title.

Queensland National Party senator Bill O'Chee said the government's refusal to publish the plan -- needed to resolve uncertainty that is damaging primary production -- raised doubts that the plan existed at all.
"The prime minister can't go around saying look at the 10-point plan, look at my clothes -- because he has no clothes," O'Chee told Reuters.

Howard is trying to resolve the competing demands of Aborigines -- who in the "Wik" court ruling last year gained rights to land leased to pastoralists -- and farmers and miners who want unrestricted use of their land.
Howard says he has a 10-point plan and discussed it with state premiers on Monday. One government source said the premiers had not seen a detailed proposal, only a broad framework.
O'Chee said Howard ought to publish the plan in time for a Thursday meeting of a committee of ruling Liberal-National coalition MPs responsible for legislation on aboriginal affairs.
"The committee is not going to sign off on some broad-brush statement of principle, because we have been bitten on native title before," he said.
"The devil is always in the detail and we want to see the detail."
Howard told reporters on Monday he would release the plan, but his office later said he intended to do so later this week.
Any government legislation has to be approved by a regular meeting of all of its members of parliament, which receive reports from committees that examine the legislation.
In practice, approval is virtually automatic but the native title issue has stirred uncharacteristic public complaints from backbenchers, especially those in O'Chee's National Party.
